archetype: small roadside church and attached cemetery complex with a legible worship program, sacral and service zoning, burial-ground organization, roadside arrival sequence, caretaker functions and a coherent long-abandonment ruin story
ground_program: roadside approach provides a recognizable pull-off, footpath or modest parking edge leading to a principal public entrance without routing visitors through graves, service yards or caretaker work areas
church interior contains a legible vestibule or narthex, primary nave or worship hall, focal sanctuary or chancel and a clear congregational orientation rather than an undifferentiated open room
sanctuary area includes a raised, framed or otherwise spatially distinct ceremonial focus with believable access for clergy while preserving congregation sightlines
one sacristy, vestry or clergy preparation room adjoins the sanctuary or rear worship zone and remains distinguishable from public circulation through placement, storage and furnishings
a small office, meeting room or multipurpose fellowship space supports administration, counseling or community use without displacing the primary worship function
sanitation and utility spaces are accessible from public or staff circulation without opening directly into the sanctuary focal area

caretaker storage, grounds equipment or maintenance functions occupy a shed, rear room or service edge with direct exterior access so cemetery upkeep does not require moving equipment through worship space

cemetery forms a coherent field of grave rows, family plots or clustered burials connected by walkable paths, with headstones and plot orientation following a deliberate site order rather than random scatter

burial ground includes at least one recognizable focal or service element such as a memorial cross, small mausoleum, family monument, cremation wall, burial shelter or grave-preparation access point appropriate to the site's scale
church, cemetery, path network, roadside arrival, drainage and any boundary wall, fence or tree line share a single terrain-seated site plan without an oversized flat platform
upper_program: if a bell tower, steeple, choir loft or balcony is present, it is supported by continuous structure and connected by a believable stair, ladder-equivalent service route or enclosed access appropriate to its function
choir lofts or balconies retain player-scale headroom, guard edges where intact and a direct relationship to the nave rather than existing as decorative floating slabs
bell or tower chambers align vertically with the tower mass and contain plausible framing, access and openings instead of unsupported exterior ornament
roof volumes distinguish nave, sanctuary, porch or narthex, tower and attached support rooms while remaining structurally coherent at intersections
upper windows, clerestory openings, vents and tower louvers correspond to actual interior volumes and lighting or ventilation needs
no surviving roof, tower segment, balcony, loft or steeple fragment may remain gravity-defying after damage derivation
circulation: public circulation connects roadside arrival to vestibule, nave, sanctuary-adjacent meeting or fellowship space and sanitation without requiring passage through clergy-only rooms
clergy or staff circulation connects sacristy or preparation space to the sanctuary and service exit without forcing routine preparation through the center of the congregation
cemetery paths connect the church entrance zone to principal grave rows and memorial elements through walkable routes that do not require stepping across grave markers
grounds-maintenance circulation reaches storage, cemetery edges and burial-service access from an exterior service route without crossing the sanctuary as its only path
where a tower, loft or balcony is intended to be accessible, it retains a supported player-scale route back to grade
damage variants must preserve at least one complete roadside-to-worship route and one viable church-to-cemetery path so the site's religious and funerary relationship remains explorable
damage_constraints: the damaged derivative must remain immediately recognizable as a church-and-cemetery site through surviving nave or sanctuary geometry, tower or roof silhouette where applicable, ordered graves, memorial elements and their shared path network

favor long-term roof leakage, timber or masonry weathering, localized steeple or tower failure, collapsed porch sections, vandalized glazing, overgrowth, toppled markers, subsidence and limited fire damage over repeated rectangular deletion masks
major structural failure should affect one coherent portion of the church at a time and preserve gravity-consistent debris, supported surviving walls and understandable load paths
if tower, roof or balcony elements fail, associated framing, walls, glazing, fixtures and debris must fail consistently so isolated fragments do not float
cemetery damage may include tilted or fallen markers, vegetation intrusion, eroded paths, breached fencing and localized ground settlement, but grave-row organization must remain inferable
do not use broad crater or trench damage that indiscriminately erases graves unless the site's explicit narrative calls for that event and resulting burial disturbance is represented coherently
preserve enough sanctuary, congregation space, sacristy or support zoning for the former worship workflow to remain legible during exploration
derive damaged, occupied, contaminated or repurposed variants only from this immutable clean master

required_manual_checks: the structure reads immediately as a roadside church with an associated cemetery rather than a generic hall beside decorative gravestones
vestibule or public threshold, nave or worship hall, sanctuary or chancel, clergy preparation space and supporting rooms form a believable religious program
grave rows, paths, memorial elements and site boundaries form a deliberate burial-ground layout with walkable access that does not treat graves as random scenery
public, clergy and grounds-maintenance circulation are distinguishable and remain functional without implausible shortcuts through sanctuary focal space or across graves
tower, loft, balcony and roof elements are structurally supported and retain usable access where they are intended to be traversable
the decay story reads as prolonged abandonment, weather exposure, localized structural failure and cemetery neglect rather than arbitrary missing cubes
at least one roadside-to-worship route and one church-to-cemetery route survive the damaged state
church foundations, cemetery paths, grave rows, drainage, roadside pull-off and boundary features meet surrounding grade without floating buildings, buried doors or a single artificial mesa
